Bought this game on SSS like 2 years ago. Playing it now and wow what a Diamond in my library.

+ Ages really well game came out 10/2014, still a fresh experience 6/2017
+ Wei fucking Shen
+ Asian GTA without being too over daunting and unfinishable.
+ Martial Arts Combat gameplay, very intuitive
+ Racing... suprisingly great controls
+ Great Story highlighting Asian values being tested
+ Asian flavored vehicles (lol): Supra, Skyline, Evo, WRX lookalikes.
+ Outfits = Asian Hero costumes! ie Jackie Chan's Drunken Fist & Rumble in the Bronx, Jet Li's Chen Zen, Black Mask, Green Hornet, Tony Ja's Ong Bak, Donnie's Ip Man, Buddhist Monk, Sun Wu Kong & Bruce Lee's Tournament outfits. Some outfits actually have signature moves like Ip Man's Wing Chun fast punches! Buy Definitive for that, otherwise those are microtransactions.

- [strike]I'm currently trying to be a completionist. 2 achievements in particular are bugged Achieve 30 Silver Stats & 30 Gold Stat Awards. I currently have 83/88 Silver Stats & 84/88 Gold Stats.[/strike]
- There are a specific 30/88 particular golden stats that count toward the 30 Stat Achievement.
- You tend to lose your gun when you start a new mission if you pick it up via open world roaming.
- [strike]I'm nearly done with everything. :( [/strike]. 
- I'm done with everything. All achievements. 100% :(

10/10

After the 100% completion I can say that:
When it comes to visual differences the Definitive Edition features better lighting, character models and textures, some improved world textures, more depth of field, smoke, smoother reflections and visual effects. In short, the game feels more organic.

Now you have more people and cars on the screen. I've noticed new faces, different outfits and generally better looks.

The keyboard keys were remapped to more standard layout. Notable changes:
-RMB to E (entering cars, countering).
-Space to L.Shift (sprint and parkour).
-RMB now is used for lock-on.

The game mechanics are mostly the same. HUD has been slightly revamped, making elements sharper, smaller. Phone's front and UI has been changed completely. Most of the icons have been changed. Main menu has activity feed now and you can switch between social hub entries without the need to wait until they load.

The car traffic AI is okay-ish, heavy trucks still scratch the walls on turns, but I've noticed that the AI sometimes keeps crashing into my parked cars. Car physics are semi-buggy. There have been cases of weird spawns and semi floating vehicles.

Pedestrian AI needs a bit of polishing. I've experienced bunch of harmless / hilarious bugs and glitches:
-Some individuals keep walking into other people as if they were walking into a wall. 
-Friendly AI had problems entering my car / locating door when needed.
-Some thugs were levitating for a brief moment.
-Panicking thugs tried to escape, got in a car and kept driving into a wall (they try to back off, but still hit the exact same spot).
-Enemy reinforcements sometimes get stuck between cars or they keep looking at you from afar.
-Random guy upstairs in Club Bam Bam went through the floor and landed on the ground floor like it was nothing.
-Some pedestrian animations keep overwriting themselves (loop too early) and end up looking like they're having a stroke.
-Sometimes people get spawned above the water.
-Some people get stuck in walls.

I've also noticed some audio issues. Sometimes some sound effects aren't played or they randomly appear / disappear. Seems like some audio bits also get either delayed or overlap (especially noticeable if happens during dialogues). Even had 2 radio tracks playing at the same time.
I'd like to point out that camera needs tweaking too. Sometimes it doesn't center well, stucks in things or points at wrong angles, has weird sensivity. Especially noticable in action hijacks.
I didn't experience these issues in original patched SD.

The DLC content is nicely implemented into the main game. You do not get instant access to the items (which would ruin the experience and challenge like in the original SD), instead you can access them in shops (the clothes guy says wacky lines about individual sets), so in-game currency has extra use now. The NANP and YOS side stories are available directly at the main menu, no need to switch between them. The red envelopes are now scattered all around the map and can be found in semi-hidden places. Notable difference: most of the DLC related side missions can only be played once, not including Zodiac island.

SWAT Pack DLC's unlimited side missions were turned into "Cop Job". No need to travel in a HKPD vehicles, the missions are marked separately on your map and unlock based on your progression. Possible scenarios (possible spoilers):
-You raid, beat up and arrest street gangs while having a bunch of officers as a backup.
-You're given a vehicle and have to ram the escaping suspect's car, then arrest him.
-You respond to store shootouts and neutralize thugs.
-Sharpshooting / one shot kill the thug without harming the hostage.

There are also some modified individual side missions (possible spoilers):
-"High Speed". Imagine Need for Speed: Hot Pursuit. You've given a police car and your goal is to shutdown a race by slamming into racer cars.
-Modified "Death by a Thousand Cuts". Arena fighting with a golden meat cleaver. Enemies have poisoned weapons and your goal is to survive and kill 30 enemies.  it's quite hardcore, especially if you haven't upgraded anything.
-Modified "Shaolin Showdown". Defeat 40 monks. Up to 30 on screen.

The optimization is even better than in the original. Playable on higher resolutions with less performance hits.
Notable difference: you can Alt+Tab freely. The game doesn't go into windowed mode anymore and stays in full screen, there's no need to change options back every time (which was extremely annoying).

Final verdict:
Worth if you've never (for some reason) played the game before.
Otherwise for fans that enjoyed the game.
PS. Needs a lot of patching. The bugs add up even if they're semi harmless.

Sleeping Dogs is an open-world game in which you play as detective Wei Shen, who attempts to infiltrate a dangerous criminal organization called Sun On Yee. To gain the gangsters' trust, Wei must follow orders, climbing the mafia hierarchy. The journey leads through numerous small and large assignments, during which you fight enemies hand-to-hand, drive fast cars, jump across rooftops, engage in shootouts, and more.

✅Very good and engaging storyline where, under the cover of being a cop, you are actually a member of the Triad
✅Character progression that really makes you want to complete every task, as it gives you additional upgrades (Police reputation, Triad reputation, and Favor reputation)
✅A large open world of Hong Kong
✅Brilliant soundtrack perfectly fitting the city of Hong Kong
✅Excellent hand-to-hand combat system (Kung Fu style), with tons of combos — and as the story progresses or by finding statues, you can learn new fighting techniques
✅For the graphical capabilities of 2014, the visuals are outstanding and really capture the atmosphere of Hong Kong
✅Huge plus of this game is the collectibles, which actually give you benefits in the story: Health Shrines (50 across the map, giving you more health), Lockboxes (providing money for better cars), and Jade Statues (allowing you to learn new martial arts techniques). I’m not a fan of collectibles that give no benefits, so this is a big plus
✅The Zodiac Tournament, where you can unlock even more martial arts techniques
✅Very diverse side missions, including police cases, different types of favors, and races
✅The game includes all DLCs as well as two story expansions
✅The "Year of the Snake" expansion is very engaging story-wise and definitely worth playing; plus, through reports you learn how Chinese New Year is celebrated
✅Spectacular and fun mechanic of hijacking cars during missions by jumping from one vehicle to another
✅Wei Shen can swim
✅Cool concept around hacking: camera hacking system, location tracking through conversations, and the "clock system"
✅Quick Time Events (QTE) during fights (I’m a huge fan of QTE, which is why I loved Detroit: Become Human)
✅Excellent price for such a great game

❌Very poor driving system, very stiff and unnatural, especially when riding a motorcycle
❌I also didn’t like the shooting system — you have a head-level crosshair, but the shots often don’t hit, plus there’s an auto-aim system
❌Bugs that forced me to repeat missions — several times during combat an enemy got stuck inside a wall and couldn’t get out, making it impossible to continue. Sometimes I also experienced strange car vibrations
❌No access to any gun shops, even after completing the main story
❌It’s a pity the developers didn’t come up with more variations of the hacking system
❌The radar didn’t work properly, it was very “glitchy,” often constantly recalculating and changing the shortest route
❌When reversing a car, the camera worked very poorly, automatically switching the view to the front of the car

[h1]What is it?[/h1]
A story-driven action adventure set in a gorgeously recreated Hong Kong setting (a mix of various Hong Kong sectors fairly accurately recreated).  The game is based on real events (though names have been changed).  You are Wei Shen, and you lead a double life as a Triad gang member and an undercover cop - so you will be playing both sides of the story.  It is Wei's job to bring down the Sun On Yee gang (a tweaked name of the real-life 'Sun Yee On') from the inside, and so he must find a way in, and get people to trust him.  Soon, Wei starts to feel divided loyalties as he gets in deeper and deeper.  The main storyline is linear but the plot is fast-paced and entertaining.  There are masses of side missions that fit in with the plot very well and you can choose when and if to play these.
 
Sleeping Dogs contains all the usual open-world elements we love: a gorgeously atmospheric and thriving city densely populated with people and traffic, great ambience (especially the night market), vehicles to unlock and drive (or simply steal), USEFUL collectibles that either upgrade your health and strength, or your bank balance!  

[h1]Is it easy to play?[/h1]
Very.  The driving and parkour elements are simple and responsive and the martial arts moves are only taught gradually and are not overly complex, though you might find yourself scribbling down a few moves as there are ultimately 12 to remember!  The game's tuition system spreads your learnt moves gradually through the game using a novel system of returning to Wei's former Kung Fu school.  For exchange of each school's missing trophies, you will be taught a new move and given some non-aggressive adversaries to practise it on.  It works very well.  As for weapons combat, I personally found it easier to switch to mouse for aiming, but the game switches seamlessly between controllers while playing.  The only negative aspect is the sometimes-uncontrollable camera angles after reversing a vehicle.  The camera is too slow to face forward, meaning you often start driving blindly.  Other than this, everything is great.

[h1]Requirements[/h1]
Regarding game requirements, you really will need to pay attention to those because this is a heavy game graphically.  There is some stutter in the cut-scenes regardless of GPU but the cut-scenes are only occasional.  You will benefit greatly from a gamepad.  This is not the sort of game for people who have a 'delicate' audience in the room as there is a lot of 'colourful' language and such.    If you're a female gamer, you'll probably cringe at some of the lines spoken by some women (some are really bad!) - but not enough to kill enjoyment of the game.

[h1]Is it worth upgrading from the original?[/h1]
If you enjoyed the game enough that you'd likely play it through again, then I'd say yes.  It looked great before but there are a plethora of improvements: denser NPCs and traffic, heaps more variety in shop signs, lots more lit signs, beautiful environment effects, super-realistic road and building textures and improved controls.  A few bugs in the original game have been fixed, and all the cars, outfits, apartments and cash DLC is no longer automatically awarded to you at the beginning of the game (a problem with the original version, leaving players with nothing further to play for).  The only caution is that, if your PC struggled a bit with the original, it will struggle more with this version given that it is a much heavier game for your GPU.

The definitive edition is 100% worth the buy, for a few extra bucks you get all the DLCs included. The average playthrough, given some side missions are skipped while some are done, takes about 10 hours complete. When completing all the side missions, it's about 15. If you just gun after the main story line, which I recommend NOT doing, you'll beat the main game in less than 6 hours. 

Certain side missions like the cop job, and even some favor missions tend to get repetitive and boring. However, they are crucial to leveling up Wei Shen, unlocking new abilities and fight moves you can utilize. I played through it twice, one skipping a lot of missions and thus losing out XP, and one where I maxed out Wei Shen's abilities ASAP. Maxing out Wei Shen with different fight moves gives you so many alternatives to destroy enemies. Killing enemies with various roundhouse kicks and bone breaks is immensely satisfying. 

Gunplay in this game isn't up to its hand-to-hand combat. It gets the job done, but there is room for improvement. The crosshair is weird and bullets seem to spray everywhere but where you point. However, the slow motion segments the game scripts into the gunfights help with that. Also - you can't carry an assortment of weapons, just a primary and a pistol - and you will lose them if the mission requires you go in empty-handed (which is almost all of them).

Story is decent. Everything you heard about this game's story is accurate. The story is good enough that Donnie Yen is going ahead to make this into a movie. Cop-Triad drama at its best.

Notable DLC is the Nightmare at North Point, Year of the Snake, Zodiac Tournament, and the "Wheels of Fury" pack. 

Nightmare at NP is a quick fun game mode, no story. Year of the Snake is following Wei Shen as a cop after the main storyline events. The story sums up to Wei Shen stopping some cult dudes from blowing up Hong Kong. Takes about an hour or two to complete. It definitely lacked a lot of features that made the main game so fun, and to lose all the different fight moves I unlocked in the base game - it was just disappointing. No new cars, no new garage, no clothing changes, no new moves - even GTA IV''s DLC offered this stuff. Basically, I got no new toys to play with and I didn't understand how this stuff was not tagged into the main game.

The Zodiac Tournament and Wheels of Fury were tagged into the main game, and they were fun to complete. The Zodiac Tournament gave challenging bosses that used a variety of new attacks. WoF gives you a fun fast car mounted with dual miniguns.

To sum it up, Sleeping Dogs: Definitive Edition is definitely worth your time. It seems like a GTA knock-off at first, but it has things GTA doesn't offer, and that is what makes this game unique.

[h2]SLEEPING DOGS 2!!?[/h2]

Sleeping Dogs is an absolute masterpiece and a true classic. Years after its release, it still stands head and shoulders above many modern open-world games. Why? Because it has a unique identity. It never tried to just be a "GTA clone"—it carved its own path with a visceral, brutal combat system inspired by Hong Kong cinema, an incredible story of moral duality with Wei Shen, and an unmatched atmosphere.

The community has never forgotten this game whenever a similar theme is shown at major events like The Game Awards, or when titles like Ananta (Project Mugen) are announced, the chat instantly explodes with thousands of fans citing Sleeping Dogs because they miss this exact essence and combat system. Sleeping Dogs is NOT GTA, so stop trying to compete with GTA. Sleeping Dogs won't sell like a new GTA, [b]BUT A SEQUEL WOULD ABSOLUTELY SELL A LOT.[/b] 

Sadly, modern publishers suffer from an obsession with trying to please a "modern audience" that DOESN'T EVEN EXIST, leading to over-budgeted, watered-down, censored games filled with boring puzzles and empty, massive maps. Sleeping Dogs proved that real players want a focused experience, with a living open world that doesn't need to be huge if it's well-crafted, bringing various mini-games and activities across the map while maintaining high quality.

If Square Enix or any other publisher ever decides to finally give us the highly-anticipated Sleeping Dogs 2, here is the gold mine blueprint for a guaranteed and profitable masterpiece:

[list]
[*] [b]MOST IMPORTANTLY OF ALL, MAINTAIN THE ESSENCE OF THE GAME.[/b]

[*] [b]Don't make the game "soft":[/b] Keep the raw, brutal environmental executions and the mature, realistic tone. The violence serves to reflect the grim reality of the criminal underworld.

[*] [b]Focus on the Police/Investigator side:[/b] Modern gaming is saturated with playing as criminals. A sequel should deeply expand Wei Shen's police work. Let us dynamically arrest suspects, respond to live radio dispatches in real-time, and investigate crime scenes dynamically and actively within the environment—without boring puzzles. The focus must be on interrogating suspects and following clues directly in the open world. 

[b]AND DO NOT CUT OUT THE CRIMINAL SIDE OF THE GAME![/b] Give more focus to the police aspect, but leave the player completely free to do whatever they want, whether good or bad. In the end, they must face the consequences of their choices.

[*] [b]Keep the core freedom:[/b] Let the player choose between a "clean cop" approach (calling for backup, using non-lethal tactics) or a brutal, corrupt, undercover approach (using the environment to extract info, keeping confiscated goods).

[*] [b]Better, not bigger:[/b] We don't need a map 4 times larger filled with microtransactions. We want the same formula, but refined with today's physics, better driving mechanics, expanded martial arts, and next-gen graphics, whether it stays in Hong Kong or moves to any other suitable setting.
[/list]

Companies just need to listen to real players and understand what they want for the profit to come. Every single day, all over the internet, there are thousands of real gamers giving valuable ideas [b]FOR FREE[/b] for the games and franchises they love. A clear example of this is exactly what I am doing right now. Just pay attention to the community and you will succeed. We are still waiting for a sequel to Sleeping Dogs.

Honestly, Sleeping Dogs is one of those games that just gets it right. Punching dudes into air conditioners, undercover cop drama, and some of the most fun hand-to-hand combat I’ve seen in an open-world game. Driving’s great, story’s solid, soundtrack slaps. And somehow, it still holds up today.
The real crime? We never got a sequel.

[b]VERDICT[/b]:
Sleeping Dogs is a hidden gem that blends martial arts combat, undercover drama, and open-world exploration into a memorable experience. It may seem similar or perhaps even inferior to GTA, but it carves out its own identity through its setting and story. I had a really great time playing it. By now I think most people would have played the game, but those who haven't should definitely give it a try.

[h3]Recommendation: ✅[/h3]

[h1]Rating: 8.5/10[/h1]

Sleeping Dogs is a nice blend of several different game genres, and while none of them are anything new or groundbreaking, everything generally played well. The original (non-definitive) version is one of the few games I have 100% completion on in my steam library.

Since you can read up on pretty much any review for the actual game, I thought I'd focus on what's new for this re-release.

The biggest improvement probably went into how the dlc was handled. Every single dlc (with the exception of the top dog booster packs) is now included, and rather than just dumping them all on you at once, they were all was integrated into the game a little better, unlocking a few pieces from each as you progress through the story. While some of the changes are minor, like a new vendor in the night market who sells some of the dlc costumes, they actually went back and tweaked a few of them to flow better. For example, the "Shaolin Showdown" side mission is no longer an endless arena where you fight until you die, but now has you running to several locations fighting smaller groups of enemies, eventually climaxing into one of the largest melee fights in the entire game. The Swat dlc missions were also changed into individual "Cop missions" that feel like they have a little more variety now and unlock over time instead of all at once. In fact, almost every mission got some sort of small tweak to it. However, Nightmare in North Point and Year of the Snake are still separate standalone stories that don't take your progress in the main story into account (though they both still unlock a few bonus items for the story when completed).

The graphics also got a bit of an upgrade, though it's not immediately obvious because the original PC game was already a big improvement over the 360/ps3 versions. Mostly, everything now has even higher-resolution textures, and there are some new effects like fog in the streets, remodeled skin and hair for most characters that looks great in cutscenes, more dense vehicle and pedestrian traffic, and some new outdoor effects. In particular, the new rain effect (and the puddles it leaves on the street) looks fantastic.

If you never played Sleeping Dogs, you really owe it to yourself to pick up this re-release, as it fixes some of the flaws of the original and includes all the dlc. However, if you already played the original and most of its dlc, you should probably skip this. Improvements and dlc aside, there is no new content (mission or story-wise) whatsoever.

Some games just hit — not because they’re the biggest, or the most expensive, but because they’ve got soul.
Sleeping Dogs is one of those.

You're Wei Shen — undercover, torn between duty and blood, walking a razor-thin line where every punch thrown feels personal. But this isn’t just another GTA clone. This is Hong Kong — alive, loud, neon-lit and soaked in a culture games rarely portray with this much respect.

And when the rain falls, and you're drifting a stolen motorcycle through back alleys after breaking a Triad member's nose? You feel it. Not just the speed — the weight.
The world reacts. It doesn’t forget. And neither will you.

The combat? Pure grit. No guns blazing. No power fantasy. It's bruised fists, snapped arms, headbutts into air conditioning units. It’s messy. Personal. A brutal ballet.
The story? Part undercover cop thriller, part tragic brotherhood tale. It’s got real heat. Real loss. No filler.

A masterpiece buried under bigger names. But for those who find it? It never leaves you.

[b][i]"Many beat their meat, but there are few who can defeat it"[/i] -Sun Tzu[/b]

[b]Story[/b]

Sleeping Dogs is a crime thriller. You play as Wei Shen, an undercover cop trying to infiltrate
the Hong Kong triads.
You are in a difficult spot. Wei is battling rival families and doing jobs for the triad all the while trying to climb the ranks of the triad to gather evidence against them.
Not only is Wei working for two different sides at the same time, but he is also losing touch between the line of good and evil. In order to keep his cover and stay alive, Wei has to do
questionable things.
It's hard not to spoil anything so let me say something cliché instead: Sleeping Dogs is a story of family, loyalty, duty, and betrayal. It may sound cheesy but it is also true.

[b][i]"You look like you could use a pork bun!"[/i][/b]

[b]Gameplay[/b]

It's a mix of Arkham City, Max Payne 3, and The Punisher.
Weapons in Hong Kong are scarce so most of the time you spend fighting with your bare fists and different melee weapons you come across. Some side activities and story missions do include shooting sections though and you can even unlock some weapons later in the game but the main focus is on melee combat.

You have your classic light and heavy kicks, grabs, and throws, but you can also unlock different combos which are pretty easy but cool to execute.
Why did I mention The Punisher though? You can do some pretty brutal takedowns.
You can literally burn or electrocute your foes. There are, of course, many more takedowns that will shock every other enemy in the fight and make them question their life choices.

The shooting sections almost play out like in most cover-based third-person shooters.
I said almost because you can trigger slow motion when vaulting over covers and it does remind you of Max Payne a little bit.  It definitely sounds like the game is trying to throw too many different things together but I'm more than happy to say that it works. They absolutely nailed their vision.
It's an open-world third-person cover-based shooter beat 'em up, parkour crime thriller action-adventure set in Hong Kong.

Did I mention parkour? Oh, yes! A good chunk of your playtime will be spent on chasing down thugs or escaping cops and to do either of them you have to run, jump, climb and vault through intense and narrow streets of Hong Kong.
Oh and if you want to find some good old collectibles and street fighting arenas then prepare to do some parkouring as well.

Driving is a bit clunky, weird and dated but you'll get used to it. It's not the worst I've seen in open-world games but neither is it as good as in GTA. The best way to describe the driving in Sleeping Dogs are the magic words: It gets the job done without problems.

[b][i]"Why don't you have a Pork bun in your hand?"[/i][/b]

[b]Conclusion[/b]

Sleeping Dogs has aged well so don't be afraid to try this "old" game out. It's a brilliant title and I guarantee you it's one of the best open-world games you will ever play.
"What about the performance?" I hear you scream while vigorously waving a delicious pork bun in your hand.
First of all, put the pork bun down. We don't want anything bad to happen to our precious pork bun. Secondly, the definitive edition came out 6 years ago so don't worry, it'll run.
Sleeping Dogs was pretty well optimized and it should run well even on a pre-historic potato tablet.
Bugs, glitches, and other silly unfixed shenanigans? None that I'm aware of. You should be fine. Just buy it and enjoy it already... And remember: A man who never eats pork buns, is never a whole man!

Honestly went in thinking this would just be another Hong Kong–style GTA clone, but it ended up being way more focused and memorable than I expected. It’s not just about playing a gangster, it’s about balancing both sides while everything around you starts getting messy.
Combat is easily the highlight. Instead of just shooting everything, most fights are up close and brutal. It’s very Arkham-style but faster and slightly more chaotic in a good way. Slamming someone into an air conditioner or tossing them into a phone booth doesn’t stop being fun, it’s weirdly satisfying every time lol. Gunplay is there, but it’s definitely not the main focus.
Driving feels solid enough, especially during chase missions. The action hijack mechanic makes things more interesting since you’re actively involved and small mistakes can cost you. Hong Kong as a setting carries a lot of the experience too. It’s dense, colorful and feels alive without being overwhelming. Not the biggest open world, but it doesn’t need to be, I’m not ready to hunt down a million collectibles anyway lol.
It’s not perfect though. Some side activities get repetitive, and a few missions lean a bit too much on tailing or simple objectives. The Definitive Edition also shows its age here and there, even with the visual upgrades.
Still, there’s a lot of charm in how everything comes together. The story sticks, the combat is satisfying and it never feels dragged out. Definitely one of those underrated games that deserved way more love than it got.

Sleeping Dogs: Definitive Edition on PC is, at its core, an exceptional open-world crime drama that still holds up years after its initial release. However, the "Definitive Edition" itself is a bit of a mixed bag for existing PC players; it mostly just bundles all the DLC with a few minor visual tweaks and performance enhancements that the original PC version already largely offered. 

What Makes It a Must-Play (If You Haven't Already)
The real star here is the original game. The story, following undercover cop Wei Shen as he navigates the brutal Hong Kong Triads, is cinematic, engaging, and genuinely feels like a great action movie. The voice acting is top-notch, featuring a celebrity cast that brings depth to the characters.
 
The combat system is arguably the game's best feature. It's a fluid, Batman: Arkham-style free-flow martial arts system that is incredibly satisfying and brutal. Environmental takedowns—like tossing enemies into a wood chipper or an electric eel tank—never get old. This focus on hand-to-hand combat is a refreshing change from most other open-world games which rely heavily on gunplay. 

Hong Kong itself is a fantastic, dense, and vibrant open world. It's not as massive as a GTA map, but it's packed with detail and unique activities like cockfighting, karaoke, and illegal street races. The city has a wonderful atmosphere, especially at night in the rain when the neon signs light up the slick roads. 

Conclusion:
Sleeping Dogs: Definitive Edition on PC is a highly recommended purchase, particularly for newcomers to the game. It's a complete package of an already excellent title with a compelling story and satisfying combat. If you can find it at a discount (which is common on Steam), it's an absolute steal and easily one of the best open-world experiences available.

Sleeping Dogs. Probably the definition of a "hidden gem" in the non-circlejerky way. The game was considered a flop by Squeenix and it flew under most people's radar. It eventually became a cult classic and is loved by many (including me!) I first played it on my Xbox years ago and decided to give it another playthrough.

Back in the mid-late 2000's, a bunch of companies were churning out "GTA clones" in attempt to rake in some cash on the new open-world crime game market. Sleeping Dogs was originally supposed to be the third game in the "True Crime" series, but since that series sucked, Activision sold the rights to the game to Squeenix. It was in development hell for a bit after that, but United Front eventually churned out a great game.

For a "GTA clone" it's easily the best I've ever played that came close to the feeling of GTA regarding the story, world and gameplay mechanics. For any fans of GTA or the genre in general, it's an easy buy. No question. 

[u]Pros:[/u]

-[b]The story[/b] is great. Kinda cheesy and very predictable, but it's fun and has a ton of likeable characters. It always makes you wanna see what's coming next. It's your typical "oh no I'm torn between my life of crime and friends or my clean life and my job" type of cliche story that tends to be the story most of these "clones" have. But it's good! It's something you'd watch in a movie and enjoy every minute. 

-[b]The world[/b] is definitely a little on the small side, but the city of Honk Kong is amazing with lots of small details scattered about. Apparently, it's also surprisingly accurate to the actual city. 

-[b]The combat[/b] is a nice twist on the usual gun-oriented gameplay that GTA and its other clones focus on. It's almost the exact same as the Batman Arkham series, if you've ever played it. Enemies flash red, you hit designated counter-attack button. Spam Button 1 and Button 2 for some fun kung-fu combos. You will be doing melee for most of the game. Guns are pretty rare in the game besides specific missions and locations. 

-[b]The soundtrack[/b] is pretty banger. Has all kinda of genres for you to enjoy while driving!

-[b]Awesome voice acting cast[/b]! They did a really good job on the voices in-game and have a few celebrities on the cast too!

-[b]Shitty karaoke minigame[/b]

[u]Cons[/u]

-[b]Some jank and bugs[/b] that go with the territory. However it's a little more prevalent in this game than the higher-budget clones. Once you play this game, and go back and look up True Crime gameplay, you can definitely see both games share a lot of characteristics, animations etc. Which makes sense, like I mentioned, this game was originally going to be a sequel for that series. It eventually became it's own game.

-[b]The driving[/b] is a controversial subject for the game. Some people like it, others hate it. I find it's... okay. It just feels "heavy". Like you're trying to drive a heavy box around, if that makes sense. The map is small enough that you don't use cars [i]too[/i] much anyways, and there's plenty of taxis around that you can use as fast travel.

[u]Overall[/u], It's definitely an awesome game and absolutely worth playing. Sadly it's very unlikely it'll ever get a sequel, but the game has aged just fine and is a blast to play. If you're somehow on the fence about getting it, just get it. You won't regret it.

As the store page for the vanilla game is only available for the DLCs it's best to summarise what Sleeping Dogs is for the newcomers. In case you only wish to know what the Definitive Edition can offer please scroll down further where I detail its characteristics.

Sleeping Dogs, in essence, is GTA in Hong Kong. You have a living, breathing city with hundreds of pedestrians, drivers and bad guys. Into this world comes Wei Shen, an undercover cop so that he can infiltrate the triads and end their reign once and for all. 

You are free to go wherever you wish in the city. Once you approach shining beacons at certain spots a mission is initiated which is introduced by a cutscene. This is the linear, the story part of the game and once a mission is complete you are back in Hong Kong where you can participate in racing events, do favors for citizens, bet in a cockfight, hack cameras, complete missions for the police, purchase clothing and vehicles. 

The activities are numerous not to mention the many collectibles scattered throughout the city: you can pay your respects at health shrines, collect lockboxes and red envelopes full of cash and you can look for jade statues to learn new moves from your old kung fu master. Oh, and you can date girls and participate in karaoke sessions, as well!

The story of Wei Shen is excellent and full of intrigue, treachery and some surprises. Voice acting is excellent but why would anyone think differently: as soon as you hear the voice of Tom Wilkinson or James Hong you know the game will deliver! As opposed to GTA, in Sleeping Dogs emphasis is on the melee combat (attacks, heavy attacks and counters - rinse and repeat) but from time to time you can get hold of several firearms, too. I like how you can utilise the environment to ease a battle: enemies can be thrown into dumpsters or into a whirling fan where they are met with gruesome death. Both combat and car handling are smooth and fast!

The 2 DLC stories that can be accessed from the main menu do not offer anything interesting, however, putting these aside in-game content requires you to devote at least 30-40 hours if you wish to reach 100% completion.

The Definitive Edition:

-- This edition gives you the full package with all DLCs included. Red envelopes are put elsewhere and some missions have been changed. In fact, the DLC clothing are now sold by a special vendor near the market area. Perhaps the most notable of this inclusion are the unique cop missions where you always assist your fellow officers (you need to hit and ram enemy vehicles or gun down bad guys or save a hostage).
-- The game has better effects and higher resolution textures. Or so they say. The former are noticeable and for a city known for its "light pollution" it is a must, to be honest. In fact, there are more pedestrians on the streets so you can really feel being in Hong Kong.
-- With all the graphics enhancements the game is still not demanding much: 60 FPS result is common, in fact, the game runs better on my rig than the original version did.
-- With new features come new bugs: audio issues (overlapping) here and there and due to the more NPCs on the streets you notice more of them get stuck at certain places for no apparent reason. Still, these are all minor nuances.
-- The game now has better keybindings. I know these can be changed in the controls menu but I always appreciate if the developers pick the applicable buttons per default. This layout now makes more sense.

To use a pun I am happy to say this edition is a definitive must! As I had already had the vanilla game in my library I got a 50% special promotion for this super package - I believe this is nice so for me this edition was an immediate purchase.

Sleeping Dogs is the kind of game that punches you in the face, throws you through a fish tank, then politely asks if you’d like to do karaoke afterward. And honestly? Yes. Yes, you would.

You play as Wei Shen, an undercover cop in Hong Kong trying to infiltrate the Triads—which basically means doing an unholy mix of police work and brutal street justice while constantly questioning whether you’re still a cop or already one of the gangsters. It’s like Infernal Affairs had a lovechild with GTA and gave it a martial arts black belt.

The hand-to-hand combat is the star here. Think Arkham-style brawling, but with fewer capes and more broken bones. You’ll be snapping arms, slamming heads into walls, and dropkicking people into phone booths with a satisfying crunch that makes every street fight feel like a Jackie Chan highlight reel. The gunplay? It's there—and fine—but why use a pistol when you can body slam someone onto a swordfish?

Driving through neon-lit Hong Kong streets feels slick, chaotic, and sometimes hilariously over-the-top. You can literally leap from your moving car onto another like a stuntman on a Red Bull binge, hijack it mid-chase, and speed off like it’s just another Tuesday. There’s racing, street fights, and yes—you can absolutely bust criminals while still rocking a knockoff designer jacket.

Wei Shen himself is a great protagonist: torn between his duty and the people he grows close to. The story gets surprisingly dark, emotional, and morally murky at times. It’s not afraid to pull the rug out from under you, even after a chill side quest where you helped someone propose via chicken fight.

Oh, and did I mention you can sing Cantonese pop songs at karaoke bars? Because you can. And it rules.

Sleeping Dogs may have flown under the radar at launch, but it’s easily one of the most underrated open-world games of its generation. It's got heart, it's got grit, and it lets you beat someone senseless with a tire iron while wearing flip-flops.

Sleeping Dogs: Definitive Edition is one of those rare games that has had my complete and total attention these past couple of weeks, and it's held up incredibly well. To begin with, the soundtrack is immaculate! I've already added many a track to my Spotify, which says a lot. Visually, it still looks amazing for its age, especially when you're cruising through the city at night and/or in the rain. More importantly, it's been a genuinely fun experience every single time I've started a session. I can already tell this is a game I might actually 100%, which is something I almost never do! That alone should speak volumes about how engaging everything feels.

The standout feature is easily the combat; the melee system is incredibly satisfying, with a variety of fighting styles like Wing Chun that give it depth and personality. It reminds me of the fighting forms from the Batman/Spider-Man games, but honestly? I think it does hand-to-hand combat even better—there were moments where I was actually disappointed there weren't more enemies left to fight! As for gunplay... it's solid, but nothing groundbreaking really. The driving and plethora of vehicles is surprisingly enjoyable and complements the open world quite nicely. Despite some very obvious limitations when up-close, the city feels alive and vibrant, with a story that's just as interesting thanks to the characters that make it easy to stay invested throughout.

It's insane to me that a game which clearly had a multi-million dollar budget, can now be bought for only $3.00. Seriously, there is literally no excuse not to add this to your library!

I remember seeing Sleeping Dogs on store shelves back in 2012 and thinking it would probably be a reasonably fun game, but I never picked it up. At the time, the market was flooded with open-world action shooters Saints Row, Far Cry, Just Cause, Assassin’s Creed, and of course the king of them all, Grand Theft Auto. It was easy for a new IP to get lost in that crowd. Fast-forward more than a decade, and Sleeping Dogs: Definitive Edition is constantly on sale for around 85% off. At just $2.99, complete with all DLC included, it’s hard to not give it a shot.

Sleeping Dogs does a great job of carving out its own niche. One of its biggest strengths is its setting: Hong Kong. Open-world games set in East Asia are surprisingly rare, and this change of scenery immediately makes the game feel fresh. While it isn’t a perfect recreation of the real city, it captures the atmosphere and overall vibe well enough to feel believable. The story also stands out, casting you as an undercover cop who must operate within the criminal underworld. This creates an interesting moral tension as you’re not a true criminal, but you’re also far from a squeaky-clean hero who always follows the rules. The game also leans heavily into its Hong Kong action-movie inspirations. Instead of relying mainly on gunplay, combat focuses on hand-to-hand martial arts, featuring a simple but satisfying combo and counter system that feels cinematic and fun.

If you’ve played other open-world action shooters, much of the structure will feel familiar. You’ll spend your time driving around the city, completing main and side missions, and choosing how you want to progress. For completionists and achievement hunters, there’s a healthy amount of content to work through without becoming overwhelming.

The game’s biggest weakness is its age. The visuals don’t hold up to modern standards, but they’re still serviceable. The driving also reflects an older, more arcade-style approach. While not realistic, I actually think this works in the game’s favor making weaving through traffic fast and enjoyable rather than frustrating. The included DLCs didn’t grab me as much as the main campaign, but since they’re bundled for free, they still add some fun variety.

My biggest personal complaint is the music, specifically the in-car radio. Since you spend a lot of time driving, the soundtrack matters, and unfortunately many of the tracks feel generic or unmemorable. I enjoy a wide range of music, but the only station I consistently enjoyed was the metal station. It’s a minor gripe, but it can be disappointing when a song you finally like comes on just as you reach your destination and it gets cut off by a mission trigger.

Overall, Sleeping Dogs: Definitive Edition is a fun and unique open-world action game that stands out thanks to its setting, story, and martial-arts-focused combat. At the ridiculously low sale prices it frequently hits, it’s an easy recommendation for fans of the genre.

Final Verdict: 8/10

Sleeping Dogs is a fun and action packed game with a brilliant story, and a great setting, although at some points it's mechanics let it down.

Story:
In Sleeping Dogs, you will control Wei Shen, an undercover cop tasked with infiltrating one of the Hong Kong triads and bringing it down from the inside. Wei himself is mostly a pretty forgettable character, and is not really shown to have many major flaws. He is tough and intelligent, and is essentially a perfect human, to a borderline unrealistic point. The story does not so much shine in all its characters as much as it does with its excellent moral conflict as Wei begins to be torn between whether or not he wishes to destroy the gang he works himself into, and in my opinion the story is one of the best aspects of Sleeping Dogs, and is a main reason I continue to return to the game. 

Setting:
While the map may be a tad small compared to many open world games, the way the streets are constructed, the sound effects, and the whole atmosphere really creates a rich setting which at least to me, never gets boring. Hong Kong is essentially a necessary part of the game due to its focus on the triads, and even though it's quite small, what they do have is done just right. While I haven't personally been to HK, a friend of mine has said that it does in fact look like the real city.

Graphics:
Sleeping Dogs is a beautiful game, especially considering how it isn't exactly too new. Some of the textures aren't too great, and often the characters seem to shine like they'd been polished, but leaving the games apartment and walking out onto a street at dusk just after some rain still never ceases to amaze me.

Music:
The original soundtrack in Sleeping Dogs, for me, isn't really anything special. It certainly isn't bad, it just isn't really unique enough to stand out. The radio songs on the other hand, really hit the mark, particularly in my opinion on stations such as Softly or Warp Radio. I never get sick of just driving around the city listening to the music.

Gameplay:
While Sleeping Dogs on the surface may look a bit similar to GTA, it is in fact quite different, something which is both a positive and a negative. On the plus side, Sleeping Dogs' hand to hand combat is very well done. While it is spammy if you want it to be, the range of options you have at your disposal means that the combat doesn't get boring no matter how many fights you are in. A downside to this combat is the presence of firearms. Guns are not introduced until about 30% through the campaign, and even once introduced you would be hard pressed to obtain one outside of a campaign mission. There is not traditional weapon select as there is in many open world games, instead you are able to carry one small firearm stored in your pocket, but that firearm does not persist between missions meaning that if you had a pistol in your pocket and then do a mission, likely that pistol will have despawned again once you re-enter the open world. The general lack of guns in Sleeping Dogs is not necessarily a bad thing however, because the guns you can use are in all honestly not always that fun. They do not really feel as satisfying as guns in, say, GTA do, particularly due to the lack of variation. While slow motion cover vaulting or quick disarms are fun, the gunplay itself is often quite lacklustre in my opinion, meaning don't come to Sleeping Dogs looking for a great shooter.

Perhaps my least favourite mechanic out of the whole game is it's driving. Cars in Sleeping Dogs handle terribly. Steering is not smooth, handbrakes are a joke, and the reversing camera is just plain bad. The redeeming feature of vehicles is the ability to jump from one to another. Despite how unrealistic doing this is, it is still satisfying to jump from one car to another in slow motion.


Overall, Sleeping Dogs is perhaps one of my favourite games of all time. It has an excellently told story taking place in a rich and atmospheric world with great visuals. The melee combat is deep and satisfying, even though guns and driving fall off a little, making Sleeping Dogs essentially a must for any fans of a good tale.

Sleeping dogs is an open-world action adventure game. The story takes place in Hong Kong were you play as an undercover cop who tries to help stop the triads from the inside out. This game reminds me of the well beloved gta games, but with a change of scenery. 
The city feels very alive and there are a lot of exotic locations. You can visit the nightmarket, temple, celebrate the new years event, sing karaoke and eat a lot of streetfood. The close combat fights are consisting of various martial arts which definitely adds to the game's theme.
You can follow two seperate story lines: the triad one and the undercover cop one. Both questlines will reward you with experience that will level up your corresponding skill tree. Besides your cop and triad level you will also be able to increase your face level by completing favors, fighting at martial arts clubs, street racing and seducing girls. 
The higher your face level the more charismatic and respected you are, giving you access to higher quality clothing and higher class vehicles. 
Besides the main story there are a lot of collectibles to be found. There are six types of collectibles to be found and some of those require you to hack camera's or crack codes on lockboxes. You can go to the karaoke bar to sing some karaoke, go to the gambling den, bet on cockfights, participate in streetraces and complete drug busts.

The game also contains two seperatly playable dlc's. "Nightmare in North point" and "Year of the snake". Both dlc's are short, but give you a completely new experience. 
"Nightmare in North point" is a horror-themed game mode that requires you to save Hong Kong from Smiley Cat and his raised army of Jiang Shi, vowing to destroy the Sun On Yee and to create Hong Kong’s most fearsome criminal empire.
To save Hong Kong, he must seek out the most powerful of Chinese magic, endowing him with a power strong enough to take on Smiley Cat’s army of Jiang Shi and face-off against the ghosts of Triads he has defeated in the past, sending the dead back to Hell once and for all.

During "Year of the snake" Wei almost immediately encounters a cult that is doing their best to usher in the apocalypse with a bang during Hong Kong's New Year celebrations. The DLC is 12 missions long and gives Wei the ability to tase and arrest opponents in combat. 

I completed the game 100% and I had a lot of fun with it. I really enjoyed the story and playing as an undercover cop even though I loved being part of the triad even more. With that being said I would rate the game a 7/10 <3

Open world games seem to have two ways to go.  You are either going to love it, or hate it with no inbetween.  It is safe to say that I am in love with this game.  The storyline alone could keep you hooked, but it is much more than that.   I have a tendency to go off on sidequest adventures to the point where I forget where I was in the main story.  Fortunately this game does not let you get that deep into sidequests as they open up while you progress the main story.   At first I was annoyed by being forced to complete missions in order to open up side quests, but in the end I appreciated the fact that I never got so into side quests that I forgot where the heck I was in the story.

What can you say about Wei Shen?  At first I thought his character was going to be this angry guy that carries a chip on his shoulder the size of China.  While he does remain pretty angry, he is a protaganist that has every reason to be as you discover in the story.  I really enjoyed the fact that he was undercover amongst the Triads and you get to see him walk that line between the law and the underworld.  I also loved the fact that you had side missions that were on both sides of the law as well.  They did a wonderful job showing Wei's struggle to do what is right over just wanting to go on his personal revenge.  Every great protaganist needs a silly sidekick, and you get that with Wei's best friend, Jackie.  If anyone watches the show Pawn Stars, Jackie's personality reminds me of Chumlee.  The voice actors were on point with their characters.  All roles were played beautifully.  Oh... Wei Shen singing karaoke is a must do in this game.  Listening to him sing Flock of Seagulls was hilarious.

The world itself is pretty big, so it took me awhile to explore every part of the map, but I have always enjoyed games where you have the ability to explore from one corner of the map to the other.  Of course it took me a few car crashes to remember that I was driving on the wrong side of the road.  After that, exploring became more enjoyable.  I went into this game blind, so I knew nothing about these random events that would pop up while you explore.  Finding some lady in a trunk of a car with lingerie on, who then proceeded to chew me out because I messed up her and her lover's fantasy, kept me quite amused.  I won't say what any of the others one are, so I don't spoil things.   

Combat was okay.  I did like that you did not have to use a gun or any other weaponry for the most part.  Hand to hand combat was effective and I didn't have to curse at my screen because I had to wait while Wei reloaded.  The reason why I just say it is okay is because it was pretty simple using a mouse.  You just clicked and clicked and you could pummel some unfortunate peon into the ground.  I did play with a controller as well, and that made combat a lot more challenging when it came to getting off combos and the like.  Wei's leveling system was pretty well designed.  He had a level system as a Triad member, as a police officer, and as an ordinary helpful citizen.  Each of these level systems had some wonderful perks, so they were all worth maxing out.  The hardest one to level up for me was for the Triads.  I had to replay some missions to get a higher score, but the police and citizen track was pretty easy.. no backtracking needed.  

There is so much to do in here, boredom just does not happen.  If you like open world games, you will love this one.  Regular price or sale price, it is completely worth the money.  I even enjoyed the DLC, which is not something I say very often about any DLC.

[h1]Sleeping Dogs – A Game That Aged Shockingly Well[/h1]

I always remembered the fighting mechanics being good, but replaying now reminded me just how well everything comes together. The game has more mechanics than you expect, and many of them feel surprisingly modern even today.

[h2]Story[/h2]

This was my second full playthrough, and even after so many years, the story still holds up. Back then I played just for the gameplay, but now I’ve started appreciating the smaller execution details, and it genuinely landed even better this time.

A few emotional moments really stood out again:

[spoiler]Jackie’s scenes still hit the same. I remembered them clearly even after all these years, so they stayed with me.[/spoiler]

[spoiler]But Winston and Peggy’s wedding scene — that one I completely forgot the details of. I knew it was coming, but replaying after almost eight years made me feel it in a different way.
It hit harder than I expected.[/spoiler]

[h2]Gameplay & Mechanics[/h2]

Fighting is as good as I remembered: smooth, weighty, satisfying, and still one of the best hand-to-hand systems in any open-world game. Parkour is surprisingly solid too, and environmental takedowns never get old — slamming an enemy into anything interactive feels amazing every single time.

Driving impressed me again:
• clean handling
• a button purely for drifting
• car ramming that feels perfect
• intense chase sequences

When the police ram into you, or when you ram into them during cases, it gives that old NFS cop-chase vibe in the best way.

Hong Kong also just feels good to explore. Compact, stylish, and full of atmosphere.

[h2]Definitive Edition Extras[/h2]

The exclusive outfits are actually more fun than expected.
• Hitman suit
• Sun Wukong outfit
• Cop uniform
• and more

They’re not just cosmetic — some give unique abilities. Sun Wukong even lets you fight with his staff. And wearing the cop uniform lets you stop NPC vehicles by shouting NYPD, and they actually give you their car. Fun little touches like that still feel fresh.

You also get the DZS-90, which looks and feels like a mini Batmobile. It has built-in guns to fire while driving and adds something new to mess around with.

[h2]Main Story Ending (Spoiler)[/h2]

[spoiler]The final mission honestly reminded me of RDR2. That monologue running through Wei’s head while heading toward the final destination pulled everything together really well.
It was a powerful, satisfying way to wrap up the main story.[/spoiler]

[h2]Nightmare in North Point DLC[/h2]

This one completely shifts the tone with a supernatural theme, and I was all in for it. I never played the DLC back in my first run, so doing it now felt refreshing. What made it even better was how it brings in characters from the main story and continues a bit of their arcs. That little bit of continuity was genuinely nice.

[h2]Year of the Snake DLC[/h2]

This was alright. Compared to the main story and Nightmare in North Point, it’s probably my least favorite, but it still has nice side missions and a few fun ideas. Worth playing once for sure.

[h2]Final Thoughts[/h2]

Sleeping Dogs aged way better than I expected. The world still has charm, the gameplay feels great in 2025, and the story hits even harder now that I understand the characters better. I finished the main story and DLCs, and this replay reminded perfectly why it’s still seen as a classic that holds up

Sleeping Dogs is one of those rare games that everybody loves, and every recommend to each other, but somehow no one has ever played it ( as far as you know).
So I picked it up during a sale after it had been sitting on my wish list for a long time, and wow. 

I get it now.

Sleeping Dogs is an incredible open world game, unique, lovingly crafted, and expertly written. Does it have its faults? Of course it does, as any game does, but the risks it takes, and the ways it succeeds far outweigh any nitpicking.

Protagonist Wei Shen is an interesting, layered, and complex main character, in a world and surrounded by characters that are just as complex as he is.
The story about Hong-Kong Triads is very well done, and every character has so much personality, that you stay curious about how the story will unfold.

I personally still haven't finished the main storyline because I simply don't want it to end. I treat myself to a story mission every now and then, like a delicious slice of cake on the weekend. 

But while the story itself is quite serious, as gangsters usually are, the story does make plenty of room for a bit of humor, and especially nods to Hong Kong action movies. 

The combat is unique and fun, the world vibrant and interesting, the characters complex, the story great.
Please play Sleeping Dogs, so you can start recommending it to your friends who will also wait months to actually do so, like you did.

Sleeping Dogs is truly an underrated gem of a game. I originally wrote this game off as a GTA clone. A bit ironic, as this game was originally released shortly before GTA V, which overshadowed this game, but I digress. Sleeping Dogs is an open world, crime drama, with a strong focus on hand-to-hand combat. You play as Wei Shen, an undercover police officer, as he immerses himself in the Sun On Yee, the Hong Kong criminal triad. An okay concept, and the story does grip you in many ways. Not the most mindblowing of stories, but it is very good for what it is. The acting and animations during cut scenes are also really solid. There are a few twists and turns that can really pull you in, and sympathize with the affected characters. The game also goes on sale for dirt cheap, I got my copy for only two bucks.

The combat is focused upon martial arts fighting, and it shows. The gun fights are rare-ish, and okay enough. But the hand-to-hand, well, it is the star of the show. Hits are visceral and kills are brutally graphic. You can learn different combos and the like to further spice up the combat. The driving is...serviceable. Not as polished as say, GTA or a racing game, but pretty okay. The setting of Hong Kong can be really pretty and nice. Its not too large of a map, but it does have a lot in it. 

This is, of course, the Definitive Edition, as the standard edition is no longer available on Steam. This version comes with all the DLC for the game. This includes multiple clothing and vehicle packs, which are all unlocked gradually as you play, instead of the instant access granted by the standard edition. The story DLC is also really fun, and adds a few more hours of content to the game. I especially like Nightmare in Northpoint, the joke DLC where, basically, ghosts and the undead invade Hong Kong, and Wei Shen must use, and I quote, "Chinese Magic" to beat up the baddies. Brilliant.

Overall, Sleeping Dogs really is a great, and often overlooked game, that you really should try. It is a real shame that poor choices left the developing studio to go under, and the sequel being canceled. Anyway, this is again, a great game. Oh, and remember, A MAN WHO NEVER EATS PORK BUN IS NEVER A WHOLE MAN!
